utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May the witness make the solemn declaration. Will you stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Apologies for starting late. There was a problem with the elevator, so it has just been sorted out and then we are able to assemble. We can start, Mr. Lukic. Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Maslic. Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are getting the translation in your head gear from the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, during the preparation for this trial, I asked you to try to respect certain procedure, and I'm referring here to the speed of your speech. This is something that I myself have been trying to do, and the interpreters have indeed often objected to the speed with which I speak. So please speak slowly so that every word will be properly recorded in the trial record, which is in our mutual interest. I also mentioned while we were preparing for this trial that you should make a pause after hearing my question of a couple of seconds and then only reply, because that too has to be interpreted. Would you please slowly tell us your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: My name is Velimir Maslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of May, 1958, in Podnovlje, Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is this place from Samac municipality, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: About 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about your parents and your predecessors. Are they all from this area, a number of generations, or did they move into the area later?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, all my ancestors lived in the area for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us whether you're married, what your marital status is? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me whether the situation in terms of your marital status was the same in 1992, and how old were your children then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In 1992 my son was 9, and my daughter was a year old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve military service, and where?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did my military service. That was in Kraljevo, in 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reserve duty station after you served your military service? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to this administration organ by virtue of my profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What educational background do you have? What schools have you completed, and when?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I finished primary school in Podnovlje and I completed secondary school in Doboj, and the two-year post-secondary school for social workers I completed in Sarajevo, at the faculty of political sciences streamed social work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you briefly describe your career? When did you find your first employment? What positions did you hold? What did your work involve? And I'm particularly interested in the period from 1990 to 1994, of course also in the period leading up to that.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was first employed in the Jakes social work and medical establishment. That was in 1981. A couple of months after that, I found employment with the Samac municipality social work centre as an officer in charge of child care and social welfare. In 1986 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"] I was elected the director of the social work centre. I held this post of director until 1991, and in 1991 my term expired, and it was not renewed, so that I was reassigned as desk officer in charge of social welfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you actually elected director? I think there was a mistake in the record.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: That was in 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, what else did you do?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Until 1992 I worked in the child protective services segment of the social work centre, and in April 1992, when the war broke out in Samac municipality, the Crisis Staff there appointed me as director of the social work centre, my duty being --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will deal with that later. Just tell me now: After that post, what did you do? How long did you remain director of the centre, and what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: So I remained on this post of director of the social work centre until 1993, the end of 1993, at which time I was elected the secretary of the secretariat for social services and administration of Samac municipality, at which duties I'm still working today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these posts, these functions in 1992 and 1993, did you hold any other positions in these years?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I'm a social worker by profession within the services of the centre I had a series of duties to perform associated with humanitarian work, primarily work with the Red Cross organisation of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hold any leading positions in the Red Cross organisation during that period, and which ones?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the president of the Red Cross from 1993, and as of April 1992 until that particular period, I had been an activist and coordinator of the work of the Red Cross organisation and of our centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were some other missions and activities that you also discharged, but we will deal with that later as we proceed with our case and your statement. Will you tell me now whether before the war you belonged to any political party.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia from -- until 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I've got the answer. Okay. So after 1990, in the course of 1991, 1992, and 1993, were you a member of any other political party?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Are you a member of any political party today?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Today I am a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: When did you become a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you another brief question to start with, and we shall also elaborate upon it a bit later. Tell me - I will not ask you whether you know Miroslav Tadic. That is totally indubitable. Tell me: Did you know Miroslav Tadic before the war, and on what terms were you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Before the war I knew Mr. Tadic by sight. We never actually socialised. I did not have any significant contacts or cooperation with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that he was the owner of a certain catering establishment by the name of the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you frequent this cafe before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I never went to the AS cafe before the war. In fact, I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps happen to hear what kind of customers frequented the place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. No. That was not actually anything that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that when you held the post of director of the social work centre between 1986 and 1991, you said that in that period, actually, you held that position of the director of the social work centre. Will you explain to us, focussing primarily on the period after the 1990 multiparty elections, how did the centre function? How many staff were there while you were there? So I'm interested in the form: How did this institution operate, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The social work centre is a social welfare institution which provides social welfare services to the population, and in so doing abides by and applies a series of laws from -- governing the subject-matter in question. For example, providing family protection and care, legal protection to families, the care and protection of minors, social welfare and protection to the population, which is in a state of social need, child care, welfare, and providing other services according to other laws. The founder of the centre is the Municipal Assembly, and the director, the director's appointment, was proposed by the assembly of the working people of the establishment in question, with the final decision on the appointment being taken by the Municipal Assembly, having obtained the sense of the departmental ministry in question. The term of office of the director was four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell me - I think I've referred to this already - how many workers were there? How many workers were employed in your centre while you were the director of the centre, and what was the ethnic mix of the population -- of the workers - sorry - which were employed in the centre?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: During my term of office, as director of the centre, there were eight workers employed there, among whom there were Serbs and Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were such centres for social work in existence in all the municipalities? What was their territorial organisation like? How were they functionally organised? Just give me this in a nutshell. Was this specific only to the Samac municipality or did they exist elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Bosnia-Herzegovina generally, about 90 per cent of the municipalities had similar centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but I'm going back to page 7, and line 12, where it reads: "During my term of office as director of the centre, there were eight workers employed there, among whom there were Serbs and Croats and Muslims." Those ethnicity terms are all in the plural, which means that there were only two or, at most, if there were Croats and Muslims, it must have been two plus two, four. So the rest -- how -- can you explain more explicitly how many persons there were of different ethnicities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Of the total number of eight employed, that is, including myself, there were four Serbs, three Croats, and one Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the interpersonal relations like in your centre? I'm talking about the end of 1991 and 1992, and I'm specifically referring and accentuating the interethnic relations within your community. What were they like?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This was a small collective, and we got along exceptionally well. We worked as one team. And there were no conflicts whatsoever on ethnic or any other grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the Trial Chamber will also like to hear this. When you -- when your term of office expired, you remained a clerk for social welfare. Who was the director of the social work centre until you were re-elected, and what happened to that particular person? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: After my term of office expired, Mr. Ivanovic was -- Djuro Ivanovic was appointed director of the centre. He was a Croat by nationality and he stayed on as the director of the centre until the outbreak of the war in Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: He left the area of the municipality. His home was in a nearby village, which now belongs to the Federation, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that he left? More specifically, when it was that he left the area of Samac municipality? The conflicts, of course, broke out sometime in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: He left the territory of Samac municipality on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at work on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. I wonder whether the witness could tell us: What was the period that this Mr. Ivanovic held his term of office as director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. How long after you -- your term of office expired Mr. Ivanovic was appointed as director of the centre? How long did he hold that office until he left, as you say, on the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, several months prior to the outbreak of the war in the territory of Samac municipality, he was the director of the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And did he speak to you about why he felt it necessary to leave the municipality of Bosanski Samac on the 16th of April, 1992, as you were colleagues, I wonder whether he discussed this with you as a director and yourself as a former director of the centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't discuss the issue with me, that particular issue with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: One last question: Did you ask him yourself why are you leaving, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have occasion to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may continue on the same line. How do you know that he left on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because once the war had broken out in Samac municipality on the 17th of April, I was already in Samac on the 19th, between the 19th and the 20th. The centre at the time was not working, nor did he appear at work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So this is a kind of conclusion you made, but you don't have any direct knowledge of his leaving on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He left work on the 16th and he didn't come back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I infer from what you just said that you were at work on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- we'll come back to the 16th of April and the events on that date, but I would like to know, because obviously we'll be discussing this issue at some length today: What was the relationship between the social welfare centre and the Red Cross in Samac? Or an additional question: Did the Red Cross exist before the war? What were the relations between the two? What were the duties of one and the other, and were they linked in any way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The social welfare centre, before the war, cooperated very closely with the Red Cross, as a humanitarian organisation, and it engaged in a number of joint activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt counsel during his direct examination. However, we've had testimony in this case about the International Red Cross, the local Red Cross. Could he just clarify which one he's talking about when he says, "We had good relations with the Red Cross," so that there will not be any confusion in the future. Because I assume when the war starts, we're going to be dealing with both. So can we just separate those two, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure counsel will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank my learned friend from the Prosecution. Perhaps this is just the right time to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you explain, in answer to this remark, which Red Cross you were referring to, what organisation it was, what was the hierarchy, who was the superior, and so on.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the local Red Cross organisation, and also the Red Cross of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that had nothing to do with the International Red Cross in those days. We'll be coming to that somewhat later. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please continue.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, we had a series of contacts and areas of cooperation, primarily with the aim of assisting the population, which was in need. We would jointly organise solidarity campaigns, which meant collecting humanitarian aid, food, clothing, footwear, and the actual distribution of the goods collected to the population that was in need. The social welfare centre and its staff members had clear records of all persons who needed assistance, and with the assistance of the Red Cross organisation, that aid and other forms of aid were distributed to the citizens of Samac municipality. The Red Cross organisation, also cooperating with the social welfare centre, the health centre, would organise various activities in the area of health care, such as, for instance, volunteer blood donations, voluntary blood donations, assistance and care for the elderly, and other needy persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you again, but referring to an answer by the witness earlier, it -- he spoke about the time before the outbreak of the hostilities. Of which time is he now speaking? Is it also the time before the 16th and 17th of April, or also during the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. My question was about the pre-war period. We'll come back to what happened later. So what you've said so far, does it apply to the period prior to the outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I understood the question as referring to the period prior to the outbreak of hostilities, and that is how I gave my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether prior to the outbreak of hostilities on Samac municipality there was anything specific regarding pre-war exchanges, and if so, did the local Red Cross organisation have any part in it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that before the war broke out in Samac municipality, an exchange was organised of detained persons on a bridge across the Sava River. I don't know exactly the date when this occurred, but I do know that the local Red Cross organisation was involved in that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what exactly the local Red Cross did with regard to that particular event?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, because I personally was not involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. For the sake of clarity, this exchange now being referred to of detained persons on a bridge across the River Sava, could we just know very briefly who the persons being exchanged were and who they were being exchanged with?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer that question, who was being exchanged for who?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the details regarding that exchange, and I did not take part in it. I do know that representatives arrived from the Republic of Croatia and that this happened on the bridge across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If that's all the witness knows, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the pre-war period, so please tell me: What was the ethnic composition of the local Red Cross organisation? How many staff members it had, who headed the organisation, and what was the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross is an organisation of citizens, humanists. There were quite a number of activists. And as far as I know, there was only one person who was professionally employed, and he was of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "quite a number of activists," could you give us a rough estimate of the number?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact figure, but I do know that every local community had persons who were members of the Red Cross organisation and who were active in the Red Cross as people who wanted to help others on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the premises of the social welfare were before the war and also the premises of the local Red Cross operation before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The social welfare centre had its premises in the immediate vicinity of the elementary school in Samac, and the local Red Cross organisation had its office in the old hotel building, which was right next to the new hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've provided an overview by way of introduction to these institutions, so I would now like to go on to certain events. So my first question is: Did you live in Samac throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in Samac before the hostilities broke out at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us of your observations of developments in Samac at the beginning of 1992, what life was like in the municipality, in the town. Were there any changes in relation to the previous period, and what were your observations of the situation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as life itself is concerned and the developments when the war broke out in Samac municipality, I can say that the situation was very tense, and there was a great deal of uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us when this was in relation to the beginning of the hostilities, which in this case it has been established to have occurred on the 16th to the 17th of April. So what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the period running up to the hostilities, because conflicts had already broken out and a war was ongoing in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and which is in the immediate vicinity of my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were interethnic relationships like in that period? Did you notice any changes in relation to the previous period?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: What changes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to life in town. Do you remember whether there were any incidents, any blockade? Did anything occur on the roads?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were incidents, and also entry into town was blocked. As far as I can remember, this was in March 1992. At that time I was not in Samac. I was attending a funeral in Podnovlje. And when I returned, I heard that the town was blocked and one couldn't enter it, and this lasted for a couple of hours. But in the morning it was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear who blocked the town and what was the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I heard that this had been done by members of Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but - I beg your pardon - on page 15, line 14, the witness said: "As far as life itself is concerned and developments when the war broke out in Samac municipality, I can say that the situation was very tense, and there was a great deal of uncertainty." I can imagine, or I can take that you formed a kind of opinion for yourself what was the reason for the situation becoming tense and fear among the people living in Bosanski Samac. Could you tell me about that, your own opinion? It must have some grounds, some reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that it was tense. I suppose that it was so because the war had already broken out in the Republic of Croatia, and Samac is a city situated quite close to the border with the Republic of Croatia. At that time already, members of the Croatian army occasionally came into town, and I used to see them in town. Another reason was that there were sporadic clashes, such as the blockade in the month of March. This is what I was referring to when I said that the situation was tense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may come with a follow-up question. Up until the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, you, among others, had lived as good friends and neighbours, together with Muslims and Croats in Bosanski Samac. So it's very surprising to hear that all of a sudden because something is happening across the Sava River or the borders of, well, to the west and to the east, that the situation became tense among those who were your neighbours and your friends up until then. Can you explain that to us? Because it's so surprising.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about this. I answered the question. I described the cooperation and the relationship that existed within the institution where I worked. As far as I personally am concerned, I had no clashes with anyone. I said that the situation was tense, meaning that that was the general situation in town, and this is what I was able to notice, to observe, as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing members of the Croatian army in town. How did you know that there were members of the Croatian army in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I know this because when I walked through the town with friends, I could see uniformed men with the insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean wearing the uniforms of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your feelings upon seeing people wearing uniforms of a different state, neighbouring state?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I felt uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question as a follow-up: Did you go in your car through the villages in Samac municipality? Did you see any changes there? What were you able to observe as you travelled through the villages?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I travelled frequently in my car to a neighbouring village to visit my wife's relatives. In the evening hours I saw that they had watch guards there. On the 16th, in the evening, with my wife and son, I left Samac and went through the village of Grebnice, which is a Croatian village, to Slatina, which is the village where the relatives of my wife live who were watching my 1-year-old daughter. On my way there I was stopped by the guards in Grebnice. They searched me, my car, and let me pass through to Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who searched you? Who were the guards?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Those were uniformed people. I didn't see their insignia. I knew some of the people from that village, and I believe that they were locals. One of them recognised me. He mentioned my name and let me pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Grebnice, what was the population, the composition of the population of that village at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The majority of the population was of Croat ethnicity. There were very few Serbs living in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were uniformed. Did they wear the JNA uniforms or some other uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Some other uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your only encounter with that type of patrol or were there any other instances of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, that was my only encounter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to another topic. Mr. Maslic, have you heard of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how and when did you become a member?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was drafted by the secretariat for National Defence sometime in February or March of 1992, and I was assigned to that unit, where I was not issued with any tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Can we please clarify the translation into English, page 19, line 12. The witness said: "I was mobilised," and not, "I was drafted." I think that we should stick to the terms that had been used before. So you said that you were mobilised by the secretariat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Maslic, you mentioned, on page 19, lines 13 and 14, that after you were mobilised and assigned to that unit, it says here that -- quoting from what you said, you say: "I was not issued with any tasks." But now, in response to this last question by Mr. Lukic on line 25 of the same page, page 19, you say that you were issued with a semi-automatic rifle. Now, I find it a little bit, you know, hard to understand. If you weren't issued with any tasks, why you were issued with a semi-automatic rifle. And I think maybe you could give some explanation. Maybe Mr. Lukic was going to ask you that himself, and I apologise if I preempt your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad to see that Judge Williams is following closely my questioning. I was about to ask the witness exactly that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: What does that mean? When were you issued with a rifle and can you tell us whether you were given any assignments, or rather, what were the instructions given to you when you were issued with a rifle?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When I was mobilised, I was given a semi-automatic rifle, but I was not issued any assignments in terms of the duties I had as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any training exercises?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of training?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings within your unit?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, no meetings whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you know who was your immediate superior? Did you have to report to somebody? Did you know who was supposed to issue instructions to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My immediate superior, my commander, was somebody who lived in my building, Mihajlo Topolovac. I asked him what my duties were, and he told me: For the time being you have no duties, and should something arise, we will call you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the ethnic composition of that detachment? Do you know any other members of that detachment and what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The people that I knew from that detachment - and I'm now referring to the circle of people that I personally knew - Ante Sapina, a Croat by ethnicity, was mobilised together with me, and another man who lived in my building. I know that there were other people of various other ethnicities in that detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position Ante Sapina held before? Did he have a position within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Ante Sapina is somebody who worked as a customs officer in Samac. Prior to that, he used to be president of the Executive Board of Samac Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the command of the 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was in the premises of the Sit factory, which was a textile factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this where you were issued with a rifle?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 4th Detachment was Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other senior officers of that detachment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know other people. I only knew Radovan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Miroslav Tadic had any kind of a position within that detachment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Simo Zaric before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight, just like Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had any particular function within that detachment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we've mentioned two of these men, let's clarify something. Did you ever, before the war, enter Mr. Zaric's apartment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. I've never been to Simo Zaric's apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We needed this clarification due to something else that has been said previously here. Did anybody from the 4th Detachment tell you anything about what was to happen in town? Did they ask you to be on alert? The neighbour, who was one of your superiors, did he give you any kinds of instructions prior to the 16th and the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When I was mobilised and issued with a weapon, I did not receive any kind of instructions regarding my military involvement. I was simply told that should any tasks come up, you will be informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Where did you keep your rifle?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I kept it in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a visible place, or did you have it hidden somewhere?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I hid the rifle under a bunk-bed in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Because my son was 9 at the time and he was very interested in these things, and I didn't want him to find the rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. One question for Mr. Maslic. You had mentioned, at the beginning of your testimony, page 3, lines 10 and 11, in answer to a question by Mr. Lukic as to what your military service had been, and that, I think, was in 1980. And you had said that your assignment was, in terms of military service, was in an administrative organ by virtue of your profession. And so I'm just wondering: In terms of this mobilisation, and you being given a semi-automatic weapon, given no instructions as to any unit you would be in or any tasks you would perform, I'm just wondering, were you given any instructions as how to use the semi-automatic rifle? I'm just a little bit perplexed, given the earlier testimony. But maybe Mr. Lukic can clarify this with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness will clarify. Perhaps the two of us understood each other, but will you please be so kind as to explain about what I asked you about your war duty station. Where were you assigned after your military service? What was your obligation there? Were you issued with any instructions, in the sense of the question asked by Judge Williams?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I said, in the first part, I replied as to my service, military service, in 1980. So this was -- I did my regular military service in that year. When I was employed with the social work centre, every conscript had his war duty station assignment given him. Every time I was not assigned to any such station as a reserve soldier, but according to my profession as a social worker, I was assigned to certain duties in the municipal administration, in the relevant municipal administration department, with the objective of my involvement if the need arose and if extraordinary circumstances called for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To contribute to your reply: In your war duty assignment that you had in the municipal administrative organ, would you have been issued with a rifle had these extraordinary circumstances indeed arisen, or any other weapon?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Had I been thus assigned, I would have probably been issued with a rifle, depending on the actual duty which would be -- to be performed by me at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you instructed in how to use a rifle while you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I was completely trained as a soldier while doing my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What actual branch were you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether that clarifies this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. I've been left with the impression that you didn't know very much about the 4th Detachment before you became a member of it. Could you clarify what was your impression of the purpose and the task of the 4th Detachment, except that it was a kind of a unit under or beside the JNA. For what purpose was it founded? What was your impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true. I didn't know anything about the 4th Detachment. Simply, I reported, having been summoned by the secretariat for National Defence, and I was assigned to that unit. As to my particular task and the role of the detachment, I didn't know anything about either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So you personally accepted to be, so to say, mobilised into a unit which you didn't know very much, at least. And then a second question: When you were issued a semi-automatic rifle, how many bullets did you get at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, I was issued with about 50 bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: The first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question was: You accepted to be mobilised into a unit about which you didn't know very much.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was mobilised into that unit and I expected that I would be given concrete tasks in the unit. I asked my immediate superior there what my tasks were, and he replied: All in due time. All in good time, you will know. When the need arises, you will be assigned your tasks. And I accepted that answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a clarification, perhaps, for Judge Lindholm. You say that you accepted. Can one at all have a choice when it comes to mobilisation, when one is called up, what are the consequences of refusing to respond to a call-up?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation ipso facto implies an obligation. There is no possibility for one to choose. There are no options. It is my duty to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to that. Number one, that's a legal opinion, or at the least, I'd ask that evidence be limited to the former Yugoslavia, that he really cannot offer any opinion as to one's right to refuse mobilisation when you have a break-up of a nation and you have a nation declares independence, you have a former country calling up soldiers from another. So I'd ask that that at least be limited to the situation under the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I would have thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without wishing to construe anything, I have a simple question, but I do have to respond to the Prosecutor. This is not in fact a legal question of that nature. Does the call-up itself specify what the legal consequences of non-compliance are? What is written on the actual call-up paper, what are the consequences if one fails to respond?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The consequences is punishment, either monetary fine or by imprisonment, but the obligation is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you accepted, you responded to the call-up of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that we have now clarified this matter. Another brief topic before I go on to the actual events. The building in which you lived prior to the war and probably also during the war, what was it like? Was it a residential house? Will you describe the flats in it and the tenants of the building, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I lived in a building, a housing -- a residential building with two entrances, with 24 apartments in it. There were 12 apartments in my entrance, and the tenants were of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your first-door neighbour by name and surname?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Hajra Sehapovic was my first-door neighbour. This was a lady. And under the storey under mine was Juro Radic, Milan Babic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Hajra Drljacic a tenant in your building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Sehapovic, so I wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. Drljacic, Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just clarify this particular point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just tell us the first and last name of this name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Hajra Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take a break and continue at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described in brief for us your building, the tenants. As far as I can conclude without leading you in any way, what was the ethnic mix of the tenants in your entrance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: It was multinational, mixed. There were Croats and Muslims and Serbs living in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me on what terms you were with your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: We were on very good terms. The relationship was very correct. We helped each other, we saw each other, we socialised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the atmosphere in the period prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already started to describe and described a number of segments of your activities on 16th and -- the 16th and the 17th of April, and we shall deal with that key period in more detail. You said that you went to the village of Slatina. Will you explain in more detail: Why did you transfer this baby to Slatina to stay with your in-laws, with your mother-in-law, as far as I could understand? Would you explain to us what happened during those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Maybe it's the translation shall but line 20 -- 19, says: Why did you transfer this baby to Slatina? I don't recall hearing anything about a baby before the break. Maybe you could clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, the witness referred to this -- his daughter, who was 1-year-old, and that is why I referred to this child as such. And now he will explain to us why he, yes, took his daughter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, "This baby" sounded like any baby, somebody else's baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I took my 1-year-old daughter -- actually, she was being looked after by a lady in town. Some 20 days prior to the 17th of April, this woman left town and went to Austria. So I had no one to look after my child, and as my wife is employed and works for the health centre, and my minor son, he was in the third grade of primary school, so I was compelled to entrust my daughter, while we were at work, to my mother-in-law to look after her, and she lived in the village of Slatina, which is about 15 kilometres away from Samac. After work, and after our son's classes, I and my wife would then go to Slatina to take care of our child ourselves and to see to -- to attend to all her needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say when this lady -- this woman went to Austria, was this an isolated case or were people leaving the municipality at this time in larger numbers?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This was not an isolated instance. People left in quite a few numbers, and those who had people abroad where they could go did leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I was in Slatina with my family that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you describe for the Court what you heard there, what happened, and what happened the next morning? Will you please explain according to what you've learned that night.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The next morning I set out for work in my car, with my wife. However, I could not pass all the way through Samac. I was informed that something was going on in town and that there was sporadic shooting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The villagers did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: So I returned, because I could not go to Samac, and I waited that day, seeing that something was happening. The next morning I put my two underage children and my wife in the car and I drove them to Cacak to stay with my sister, because I thought that they would be safe there. And after the situation calmed down, we would be able to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I need clarification on two points from your reply. First of all, who prevented you from going to work, from going into Samac? Who told you that you couldn't? And please explain to the Court where this Cacak is.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When I set off from Slatina, the road which leads via the village of Grebnice, somewhere at midpoint on that road, I was stopped by a soldier, a local villager, and he told me that I could not go on towards Samac. To my question why I couldn't, he said that there were shooting there, that it wasn't safe. And in particular, in the vicinity of the village of Grebnice, which I had actually passed through the night before and where I was stopped. So I complied, and the next day, as I've already described, I drove my family to Cacak, which is a town in Serbia, some 300 kilometres from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, together with my wife, I set out towards Samac, leaving my children in the custody of my sister, intending to report for all my duties. My wife was a medical worker herself, and so she accompanied me on this trip in order to report for work at the medical -- at the health centre. So we -- I arrived in Samac, in my apartment, and spent the night there, and spent that night there. When I arrived in my flat, or rather, at the very door to the flat, Juro Radic, a neighbour of mine, informed me that my flat had been broken into and also that all the flats which were currently uninhabited had also been broken into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What is this Juro person by nationality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Juro Radic is a Croat by ethnicity, and he told me this, and then he accompanied me to my door, and also told me that he had shut the door and tied them -- tied it with some wire, because the door had been broken down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who had done it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: He told me that some men in uniform, as he said, some people in motley uniform, had done it. He didn't know them. They were masked. And he said that these were the men who had broken into my apartment, among others. With my wife and this neighbour of mine, I then entered the flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. You said some people, some people in uniform, as you said, some multicoloured uniformed people, in motley uniform. Just some more clarification, please. Did he tell you why they had done that? Why had they broken into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: He told me that all uninhabited flats in which there were no people could unlock the doors had been broken into, the reason for that being that perhaps there could be some people in those flats who had arms or could shoot from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find when you entered your flat?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When I entered my flat, it had been completely ransacked. All -- everything from the wardrobe had been on the floor. The furniture had been removed. The whole place had been ransacked, in a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Maslic, just for sake of clarification, as I understand it, you've said that you, together with your wife, returned to Samac on the 20th of April. Correct? Okay. So your next-door neighbour, or the neighbour that you mentioned here in your responses to counsel's questions, Mr. Radic, I believe his name was, did he indicate when exactly your apartment was broken into? Obviously it was before the 20th of April, but do we have some more clear indication of when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the apartment on the 16th, but I wasn't there on the 17th, 18th, and 19th. He didn't tell me exactly which of those three days the flat had been broken into, so I can't answer that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So from your answer, then, we can presume it was the 17th, 18th, 19th, or the 20th, before you actually returned there; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: A follow-up question here: In which part of the town is your apartment or was your apartment located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apartment was in Pere Bosica Street, number 50, so it is in the very centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: How far away from the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer to Judge Williams's question does not appear in the transcript. The question does, but not the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She asked you, from your answer, we can presume it was the 17th, 18th, 19th, or the 20th before you actually returned there? And your answer to that was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since we're discussing this: Was your surname inscribed on the door of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, my first and last name was written there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Is Maslic a Serbian surname?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling us what you found when you entered. What about your rifle?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The rifle was hidden in the bunk-bed in the kitchen, and it wasn't found, so I found it there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people who ransacked the apartment hadn't found it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, they hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether anything had been stolen?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. Nothing was stolen from the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you have a telephone in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the other apartments also had telephone lines in your building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. All apartments that you reached from my entrance had telephones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, did you notice anything unusual about the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The telephone line was cut. It wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the telephone in the neighbour's apartments?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Judging by what I heard from other neighbours, their telephones weren't working either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, once again. Just again a point of clarification. Before the break Mr. Maslic had said, on page 32, lines 13 and 14, in response to your question as to what he found when he entered his flat, he said that everything was on the floor, et cetera. Then he said: "The furniture had been removed. The whole place had been ransacked, in a word." But now, in response to one of your questions -- I can't find the exact line here now. Oh, yes, I can. Page 34, your question, line 3: "Did you notice whether anything had been stolen?" The witness, if the translation is right, so that's why I need the clarification, line 4, says: "No, nothing was stolen from the apartment." So this is rather at odds with what we heard before the break concerning all the furniture having been removed, for example. So can you clarify that? It seems to be inconsistent. So it's page 32, lines 13 and 14, re: The furniture having been removed. And now -- well, what I've just said, line 4 on page 34, concerning nothing having been stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's an error in the translation. The witness said that the furniture had been moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's clarify this. Was anything taken out of the apartment, or was it just moved around?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Nothing was taken away from the apartment. Things had been thrown around, scattered, and moved around within the apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that makes sense, because there's a big difference from removed and moving around. So that makes sense now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to this story about the telephones. I would like to know whether during the war, did your telephone line start working again? If you don't remember exactly, tell us approximately.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I do know that throughout 1992, the telephone in the apartment did not work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did any of the telephones of your neighbours work during that year?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned to Samac, did you listen to the radio? Do you have a radio and did you listen to any announcements broadcast over the radio?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I didn't listen to the radio, because I didn't have any electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you that, what the situation was like regarding electricity in that period of time and generally during the war.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In that period of time there was no electricity, no running water. We used artesian wells for water supplies, and there was only one such well in town, so the situation was very inconvenient, very ugly, without the essentials for normal life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently would the electricity be supplied?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: At first there was no electricity at all, and the water would come occasionally, because there were generators working with oil, and they pumped the water. So during the day there would be periods of one or two hours when the water supply was restored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did electricity supply become more regular?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but in the course of 1993 there was more electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then, when you arrived in your apartment, looked around and saw what had happened?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: My wife went off to work. I was asked by Mitar Mitrovic to go to the Crisis Staff, which handed me a decision saying that I had been appointed director of the social welfare centre, and he explained to me that I should do my best to make sure that the work of the centre and the Red Cross be organised properly to ensure the basic conditions for the normal life of citizens. This was my duty also, pursuant to the law on social welfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where the premises of the Crisis Staff were at the time? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I went to the premises of the Uniglas factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of the Crisis Staff prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else when you went to see Mr. Mitrovic and received that decision?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I only saw the security guard, people I didn't know. I didn't really know Mitar either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know him from before?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know Mr. Simeon Simic? [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. Simic"]

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him on that day there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction, please. On page 37, line 17, my question was Mr. Simeon Simic, and the witness said yes, and that he didn't see him on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Blagoje Simic as a physician working in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him there on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You mentioned your wife, saying that she went off to work. You said that she worked at the health centre. What was her position, and did she work there throughout the war? Was she with you throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: My wife worked as a senior nurse in the health centre for vaccinations, and she reported to her director, who assigned her to the same position she had held before, and she held this position throughout the war, with the exception of a few months, when she went to visit our children in Cacak. And this lasted for about two or three months in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that did she come back?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, she came back and continued her -- resumed her duties, duties that she is performing to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a minor intervention to make. The witness said that she reported to the director of the health centre. His name is Mesud Nogic. And when did your children return to Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As I didn't have the proper conditions to look after the children in Samac, the school was not working in 1992, so it was only in 1993 that I brought the children back from Cacak and put them up with my mother in the village in which I was born. My son went to school there for half a year, for two terms. And the second half of the year he came to Samac and continued his education there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why didn't you bring your children to Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I didn't have the appropriate conditions. There was no electricity, no water, and the school had been burned down, the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Samac shelled during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Samac, the town itself, and the settlements around Samac, were shelled on a daily basis, and it wasn't safe for children to stay there under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the elementary school had burnt down. Tell me: Where were the premises of your social welfare centre before the war, and where did you organise the work of the centre from the 20th of April onwards? I'm talking about the social welfare centre.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I have already said earlier on that the premises of the centre were very close to the elementary school. In view of the fact that the school had been torched on the first day of the war, the premises of my own institution were devastated, and it wasn't possible to work there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you go? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Once I received the decision regarding my assignment, I went to those premises. But before that, all my associates who were in town, I called them and we went together to collect the documents from the centre to preserve all the files, which were very important, and files and binders which are important for an institution of that kind. And I addressed the secretary of the local community at the time, Mr. Bolasevic -- Bolasevic Zeljko, and I asked him whether I could use for the social welfare centre premises in the building of the local community offices. Why did I choose that particular building? Because I felt that this building was the safest and that it had enough space for me to be able to organise the whole service of the social welfare centre and the Red Cross organisation. And Mr. Bolasevic opened the offices for me, two offices, actually, that used to be used by the employment bureau at the time, and it was in those offices that we placed the archives of the centre, which we had managed to save entirely, and we continued working in those offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you enter those offices alone or were some people using them when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, there were no other services there, but there was sufficient space. I think there is altogether six or seven offices and a conference room which could seat up to 30 people, quite enough for several services to operate in those offices. Those offices were on the first floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a very interesting topic, so we'll discuss it later. But talking about those first days of the war, let me ask you: Had you heard of any order for people to wear white armbands in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I never heard of any white armbands, but in town I would see soldiers every day who had certain ribbons on their lapels, but the ribbons were different every day. Sometimes they were white ribbons. These were people in uniform, wearing these ribbons on their lapels. Now, what the meaning of those ribbons were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to leave the door of your apartment unlocked at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I did not have to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether other apartments in your building had their front doors locked in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: When I would come back from work in the evening, since we had no electricity, our neighbours and we would sit together in the stairwell, because that was the safest place. Naturally, after that everybody would go to their own apartments and lock the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that the safest place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Due to shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn back to the re-establishment of your social welfare centre. You told us about your efforts to put in place your staff. Can you tell me how many workers you had and what was the ethnic composition of the personnel that worked in the social welfare centre?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I attempted to establish the service by employing professionals who used to work in the social welfare centre. In addition to that, I also tried to engage people who wanted to get involved in that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of the personnel?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The people working there were of various ethnicities, mostly those who were not fit for military service. There were Muslims there, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But using those people who used to work in the social welfare centre before and were still available now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And how many workers did you have there? Do you know the approximate number?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but I think that I had about 20 people employed there, discharging the duties within the social welfare centre and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the offices of the social welfare centre remain in that building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the date, but sometime in 1993 we moved out of those premises into other premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell me this. I'm interested in that particular building. What other services, in addition to your centre, were housed there in the beginning of the war, and tell us who had offices on the ground floor and what institutions had services on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: That building is known as the hall of retirees. On the ground floor there's the club of retirees. That is a cafe where the retired persons can play dominos, check [as interpreted], have coffees and tea and so on. There were two offices on the ground floor, and as far as I can remember, in 1992 they were occupied by people who assigned people to various work assignments. I think that there was Celic Dzevad there, and I think a man with the last name Kapetanovic, nicknamed Beg. On the upper floor of that building, in the premises of the former employment bureau, the centre for social welfare and the Red Cross were housed. Later on, next to those offices is where the civilian protection staff was housed as well, as were staff members of the local commune who occupied their own offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "later on," how much later was it? When did the civilian protection staff relocate there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many days later, but very soon after our arrival there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could photographs D36/3 and D38/3 ID be shown to the witness, please. Can we please see D36/3 first. We will put it on the ELMO, and then you will be able to see it on the screen. Mr. Maslic, do you know this building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This is the building called the hall of the retirees that I spoke of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please take the pointer and show us whether you can see the premises of the pensioners' club and whether we can see here the offices of the work obligation service.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: These premises here were held by the pensioners' club, and the entrance was here on the street, whereas this place here is where the offices of the work obligation service were. The entrance leading to our premises was on the other side of the building, and then upon entering there we would have to go to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness has shown the ground floor, the right corner of the ground floor, which is where the pensioners' club premises were, and then the middle part, between the white and the green vehicle, is where the entrance into the offices held by the work obligation services were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Presiding Judge please confirm that this description was accurate? Can we put it for the record in this manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought the witness had agreed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted the Presiding Judge to confirm that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell us whether, from this angle, one can see the offices of the centre and the premises of the Red Cross and civil defence and the local community.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the entrance leading to those offices is from the other side of the building, from the courtyard. The premises of the centre and the Red Cross are here, this window, and this other window. The offices of the civil defence are here, behind this window here, whereas the local community premises are behind this window and on the other side of the building, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, could we please indicate that the witness has shown the windows on the first floor, behind the white panel, as the offices of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These two windows here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the left of that, whereas the offices to the right of that, were those of the local community and of the centre?
