utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that was correctly described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown D38/3 ID, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This is the hallway on the floor where the offices of the Red Cross and the centre were located. These are the offices of the Red Cross and the centre. And here are the toilets. And this door here leads to the premises of the civil defence and the local community. There's a hallway beginning here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, let us say that the witness has indicated the right door on this photograph as the door leading to the offices of the social welfare centre and the Red Cross, whereas to the left, the door there leads to the toilets, and the other door leads to the hallway, which then leads to the offices of the civil defence and the local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since one of the witnesses did not recognise this area here, this photograph remained as an ID document, but now we would like to tender it into evidence, because this witness has recognised the floor where the offices of these services were. I would like this photograph to be recorded as the photograph depicting hallway leading to the offices of the Red Cross, social welfare centre, local commune and civil defence within the pensioners' club building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the number confirmed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D38/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, briefly, please: You told us that you were director of the social welfare centre. Do you know who was the commander of the civil defence staff then, from the beginning of the war and onwards, and who, as commander of civil defence staff, used the premises next to yours?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: These premises were used by civil defence staff. The commander of the staff was Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Who at that time was president of the local organisation of Red Cross? I assume that person was called "president." So who was the leader of the Red Cross in April and on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Milorad Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The premises held by the work duty service on the ground floor, did they have any physical contact with the offices on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. There was no physical link between these offices. They had two different entrances which were located on two opposite sides of the building that I've shown on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one enter the building from the offices of the work duty service or did one have to leave the building and then enter through the other entrance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: One had to exit the building and go to the other entrance, around the building, in order to reach the offices of the work duty service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning of the war, did these offices have telephones, I mean 1992, when you were there in that building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross had a telephone connection, and there were very few telephones that were operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that telephone situated in the offices of the Red Cross and the centre? Were those joint offices?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The telephone of the Red Cross was in the premises of the Red Cross, and I think that the civil defence service did not have a telephone at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a telephone at your centre? Did you have an operational telephone then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I said the Red Cross, but our offices were joined and our service was -- we had a common service, so only one telephone. So it was also our telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another telephone on that floor that was operational?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The offices of the work duty service, did they have an operational telephone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, concerning the telephone, do you know whether other people came, whether they asked to use it? How was it used?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Since that was one of very few telephones that was operational, a lot of citizens came in requesting to use it, and it was used by the citizens in order for them to be able to talk to their relatives and so on. I introduced a rule that -- allowing them to use it early in the morning for brief phone calls, before we started working. We received a lot of requests, and I think that all of those who applied to us asking to use the phone were granted permission, but only for brief calls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why only brief calls?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Because we had many requests and our time was limited. And they were allowed to use the phone, but due to numerous demands and a limited amount of time, the calls were brief. They could only call briefly their relatives and give basic information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of all three ethnic communities come to use the phone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I can tell you that Kemal Omeragic used to come often to call his brother, because his brother Fikret was wounded and was in a hospital in Belgrade. He used to come every day to make phone calls to inquire about his brother, who later died. Not only him; there were other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Your Honour, could we have some clarification as to the time period that we're dealing with as to the telephone issue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please respond to this OTP remark? How long did the telephones operate in this way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This was some time in April, May, or June, and later there were other telephones that were put into operation, but this was the situation. It was mainly in 1992 that the situation was like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "1992," you mean until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as the social work centre, get a telephone by the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: But we had a telephone there at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant apart from that one telephone which you had, did you get any other connections?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. We just had that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, shall we now turn to the activities which you undertook then? What were the first tasks of your social work centre and what is it that you did during those first days?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In view of the very unfavourable situation which obtained in town, there was no electricity, in other words, there was no water, and there was no supplies of the basic staples or basic foods, and of course the population that was in town was in dire need of such foodstuffs. We had been given data earlier, information from the centre of social work, from the beneficiaries of the services of the social work centre. I don't think I need explain who these were. We had quite a lot of children who needed milk. On the basis of such preliminary records which had existed already in the centre, previous, previous records, and the new records which were compiled by our own activists of the Red Cross chapter, we actually identified the requirements in milk and bread. There was no milk to be had in the local stores. What we did was to organise the milking of cows in an agricultural estate and the transportation of thus obtained milk by a Red Cross vehicle, which we did twice a day, in the morning and in the evening. The collected milk was then distributed by points, at four points in town, where the need was the most acute. We distributed the milk according to the quantity available at the time. However, as the number of those who needed milk and bread was very large and increased, in the first -- in the initial period we -- the distribution took place in a rather -- was carried out in a rather spontaneous, so to speak, fashion so there were some abuses on the part of some of the citizens, and other people were unable to obtain or could -- never -- their turn never came to get some milk actually objected. So that after a couple of days of such practices, I sat down with my associates and the activists of the Red Cross chapter to address the situation, and we agreed to control the distribution of the milk to -- of the -- to the users --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can we avoid these details that are not necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I let the witness describe this because I intend to introduce a number of documents which specifically refer to the distribution of milk and bread and the initial organisation of that distribution, and some reference to this has already been made in the Prosecutor's case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Maslic, we shall now quickly review a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have prepared a number of documents, and I wish to now present to the Chamber these documents which we wish to ask Mr. Maslic about. Every document has been internally marked to correspond with that of the Prosecutor, so the order will actually follow the marks, which I will always initially indicate. The first document which I wish to be shown to the witness bears the internal mark BDB 4/3. Will the usher please show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I presume, actually, that's an error in the transcript here on line 6, where it says "BDB" it's P, P for Peter or whatever; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My initial consideration was actually pre-defence brief that is why I actually put these initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks for itself, and I will only ask you briefly: Whose signature does the document bear?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The president of the then Red Cross chapter, Mr. Milorad Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can see your name under serial number 1. Were you an activist of the Red Cross at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war and at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ethnic composition was of the persons who are on the list?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: It is different. You can see that they are Muslims and Croats and Serbs there. Of course, I can indicate these individuals as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Just count them. Tell us how many Serbs, Croats, and Muslims were there.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: There are 11 Muslims, and the Croats also?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Anka Jovanovic. One Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Marko Nogic a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me: Next to this name under serial number 18, there is the indication minor. How old was this person?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was, but I know that he was under age and that he was an activist of the Red Cross, that he had been an activist of the Red Cross also before, and that he had been very active and very dedicated, and that is why we also recruited him to work for the Red Cross at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I wish to tender this as an exhibit, this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D85/3 and D85/3 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If I may as well ask the Prosecution, because they received all these documents: Are there any which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection to any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So we'll simply be going ahead with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document marked PDB 23/3, please. This is a list of women going to Pisari to milk cows on the 9th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Previously you referred to the organising of the milking of cows via this agricultural estate, but what is this specific document about? Does the civil defence staff organise any other activities relevant to the -- I mean, sorry, the staff of the Red Cross relevant to the milking of cows?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: We drew up this list because the Ministry of Defence issued a decision to the effect that such persons were to be recruited for this particular activity in order to enable them to go and milk the cows in this place outside the city without any hindrance. This was intended as a pass for them. And, on the other hand, the vehicle of the Red Cross was at the same time used as a civil defence vehicle, and the driver was Ismet Hurtic. So that we submitted this list to both the civil defence staff and to the police in order for them to be able to monitor the transport -- the movement of the vehicle in question and also to know what individuals were concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was this to be submitted to the -- why was it submitted to the secretariat of defence?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Because it was the secretariat that had issued the decision assigning these people to their respective work duties. These people -- these individuals had the obligation to work on the basis of the decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at this list? These are all women, as far as I can see. Are there members of all the three nations here?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there are. There are Muslim and Serbian -- Serb and Croatian women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What then happened to that milk? Who distributed the milk afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the milk which was milked? Was it used privately or what?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No. The milk would be transported in special containers, in special barrels, and it would then be distributed to different points in town. There were four such milk distribution points in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, can we be allocated a number for this documents. And we hear that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 86/3 and D86/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another document. Can the registrar please repeat this number? It is not on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Certainly. It is D86/3 and D86/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document which I marked PDB 13A/3, 13B/3 and 13C/3 and I believe that in view of the content of these documents, these are very useful and they should be held under a single number because this involves the distribution of milk by city section, and they are of the same date, which is the 23rd of May, 1992. And in the right top-hand corner you have an indication of the section of the city involved. I will remind the Chamber that there is a document which has already been tendered. I believe it is 47, this district 4 [as interpreted], I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Could you maybe just look at the transcript there, page 55, line 1? You say: "I believe it is 47, this district 4." Maybe you could just clarify that, just briefly, because I'm not too sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was mis-recorded in the record. This is all my fault by wishing to expedite the procedure perhaps. What I wanted to say was -- document, an identical document which referred to the 4th district in the city of the same date, the 22nd of May, has already been tendered as document marked - and I will tell you exactly in a minute - it was in respect of the witness Hajra Drljacic, and the mark of the document was D44/3. And I did not consider it necessary for us now to show that particular document to the witness. It is part of the same group of documents, and I didn't want to tender all the documents with Mrs. Drljacic then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, please look at it. Do you have all the three city districts, city sections, before you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the second and the third document, the first, the second, and the third documents. What do these documents show?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: These lists demonstrate, first of all, what persons were using bread and milk, the number of household members, the quantity of bread, the quantity of milk. These quantities were determined according to set criteria, which I've already described in my previous part of this statement, and we drew up lists like these on a regular basis and informed thereon the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a quick look at the list. I'm interested in the national, the ethnic composition of the persons on these lists and whether there are any -- the predominating members of any particular nationality.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: You can conclude on the basis of all these four lists that the users of these foodstuffs were, as a rule, most of them were Muslims, which was only logical, because it was predominantly Muslims who lived in town. The Muslims lived, as a rule, in town and were unable to obtain such foods in other ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards this district number 3 under serial number 15 in the list, do you know who these were?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any relation to Mr. Salih Hibilic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, if there are no objections, could we be assigned a number by the registrar, please, for these three documents, and they can be then tendered then cumulatively. Just to correct my question, the actual name of the person in line 56 [sic] was Ibrahim Salkic, page 56, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D87/3, A, B, and C. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one will be A, B?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first list marked by counsel is 13A/3. He has maybe a number 65/92, is A. D87/3A. The list with number 66/92 will be B. And the one with number 67/92 will be C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, after this first distribution of milk and bread in May, did any problems arise over the distribution, and could you very briefly tell us about those problems?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that at first there were some problems because the demand was high and the quantities of milk were small, so we had to establish certain criteria on the basis of which we would focus on people who were really in need and just those needs to the available quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the criteria?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The criteria were, and with my associates, I relied most on the law on social welfare and the law on child care, child welfare. We gave priority to the elderly and the sick and the children, that is, to those persons who had no income of their own, so that the social factor had the highest priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit D43/3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I've spoken about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see the date is the end of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these criteria observed? Is that how you distributed these staples?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to discuss this document any further. I asked you about your centre, and now I'll ask you about what the Red Cross did in those first days, specifically how it distributed humanitarian aid, not only in the first days of the war but throughout the war. What humanitarian aid actually meant, how it arrived, and how was it distributed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As time passed, the needs became ever greater, and the stocks in the Red Cross warehouses became smaller. So it was essential to engage all the activists of the Red Cross and all others who wanted to assist to provide as much aid as possible so as to ensure essential foodstuffs. Before the war reached Samac municipality, there was a number of refugees already from Croatia, and in the warehouse there was some aid, some supplies, which I assume got there from the Red Cross of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But these were small quantities that were quite insufficient for such a large number of inhabitants. At the time, within the framework of the centre and the Red Cross, we organised ourselves in the form of several commissions or services - the name really doesn't matter, whatever we liked to call them - and one of these commissions had the task of collecting humanitarian aid, which meant going to Belgrade, to the Red Cross of Yugoslavia headquarters. And it also implied appealing to our own citizens' donors who were ready to contribute. So another group of people were in charge of the distribution of that aid. And the third group or service was in charge of health care. I have to point out that Samac municipality is one of the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had a very pronounced problem with endemic nephritis. It was second in Bosnia, and just before the war a haemodialysis centre had been built in Samac, and in that centre, dialysis treatment was provided for about 100 patients, who would visit the centre three times a week for treatment. The reserves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've already got evidence on dialysis treatment and that it was endemic in Samac. I don't think the Prosecution are disputing that. The Prosecution, on the dialysis treatment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to refer to this as exhibits have already been admitted into evidence, and this witness was directly involved in ensuring the equipment and in providing the devices. And you remember perhaps that in the defence case of Mr. Simic, there was a document signed by him, so I wanted to touch upon the activities linked to that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to clarify the problem, because it was far more difficult to ensure dialysis treatment than food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Simply going directly to the documents without telling us how many patients were there, how many times they received this treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown document D109/1 so he could comment on it and refer to it. It is a report on the activities of the Red Cross organisation and the hospital in collecting aid for the haemodialysis centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, I think you know this document. It is self-explanatory, so you don't need to summarise it. Just please tell us: After this visit you made to Belgrade, because obviously you were one of the authors of this document, what happened? Who did you have contact with over there and what were the consequences of that trip that you made to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document, and it speaks of one of a series of my visits to the Red Cross of Yugoslavia and the contacts -- together with doctors who were working in the hospital at the time, and this was one of the problems that we addressed with the World Health Organisation. They had their offices in Belgrade. And that is when I met Dr. Warry [phoen]. He was the head of the office there and he had heard of the problem with dialysis in Samac, probably from the Red Cross of Yugoslavia. And on that occasion, that is, on the occasion of our visit with Dr. Warry, he said he could do nothing to assist these patients because the World Health Organisation dealt exclusively with the problems of the injured and wounded in the war, that these were chronic patients, and according to their rules, they could not assist them. However, he gave me some hope and said that his associates would come to visit Samac to see what the situation was for themselves and that he would raise the issue at a higher level. And indeed, a couple of days later a delegation did arrive of his associates. They brought with them at the time some dialysis material. And as far as I know, from then on a system was established of the providing supplies for dialysis via Vrsac Hemo farm. I think that is the name of the factory manufacturing dialysis equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, just one more brief question. Regarding the distribution of humanitarian aid, were there any problems with the distribution, certain unevenness in distribution at the level of local communities? Was anything done to address the problem?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were sporadic problems would arise, people that were dissatisfied. They wanted more. And sometimes certain activists did not give them the aid intended for them. But it is only logical that such problems would arise, in view of such a large number of beneficiaries. But they were addressed, and my associates and myself would get involved and remove the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the appropriate time for the break as we are moving on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our break and continue at 1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should now like to examine briefly with the witness the locations of some buildings on a map that we have used in this case, and I would also like the map that has the number D27/3 as the identification number to be given an official exhibit number. You will probably remember that after Esad Dagovic said that there were certain inaccuracies on that map, the Trial Chamber asked me to obtain authentification of that map, and I addressed the republican administration for Geodesia and I received the expert opinion of that institution, and I have already provided the Prosecution with a copy of this map, together with the expert opinion on it. I have the original, with the stamp. I can provide Your Honours with a copy and an official translation. In my view, there are two minor discrepancies, and I have discussed this with the Prosecution and they have no objection that the map that we have been using should be admitted into evidence. So I have five copies of the map. The expert opinion of the administration and the official English translation. So you will see the discrepancies that they have identified, namely, they believe that the buildings were in a larger scale than the real situation, and there is a small blind alley that hasn't been drafted on the map. They have given me their official map, which is very clumsy for you, since it is about two metres large, and I think it would be very inconvenient for use in court, but I hope that with this expert opinion there should be no problems with this map. And Mr. Di Fazio is familiar with all this, and I don't think there should be any difficulties. I would also like to hand Your Honours the original, with the stamp of the institution, because on the copy the stamp is not visible. So I have the original text in the B/C/S version with the stamp on it. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, when I spoke with Mr. Lukic - he may be able to set us straight - I thought there was a problem with the location of the Municipal Assembly as depicted on this map. That could be important. So I think if Mr. Lukic could explain the mistake made with respect to the Municipal Assembly, we should be clear about that. Other than that, I've got -- the Prosecution has no problems with the map being produced into evidence once that issue is clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be seen from this report that the building DPO, which is in fact the building of the Municipal Assembly, if you look at it on the map, it has been marked in Marsala Tita Street, and according to the report of this administration, that building shouldn't be there, but it should be to the left of the hotel. So the hotel is across the street, and it should be next to the hotel. That is their observation that they have made. No. The mistake that they have identified on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO perhaps? And if the witness is going to point --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I approach the ELMO, please? Do you wish me to show it on the map? Or perhaps the witness can explain it. Maybe that would be the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, will you look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And next to that building, it says "SO," doesn't it? Is that the Municipal Assembly building? And next to that building, it says "DPO," to the left.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the report of this land surveying administration, the DPO building should be next to the old hotel.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Municipal Assembly building is correctly marked next to the SUP building. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So can the witness leave the pointer on the correct place where the Municipal Assembly building should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Is it to the left or the right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because by the time the translation comes in, the pointer is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. This is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We were told that it's next to the hotel. What is next to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: To the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no dispute regarding the Municipal Assembly building. It is this building marked with the letters "SO" that the witness is pointing to right now. That is the Municipal Assembly building, and it is correctly marked. Next to it, to the left of it, the building marked DPO should be next to the hotel. Or rather, the marking of the hotel is next to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness confirm this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could mark it with numbers to make things quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's clear with the Prosecution, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. No problem. The only issue that we have is, D27/3 has been marked by one witness, the exact same map, D21/4 has been marked by a second witness. And if we're going to introduce this third map, even though they're all the same, they should reference each other, I think it should be given a separate number as opposed to D27/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It should have a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's all. No other objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to have a new number or are we going to use the same number, D27/3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We're going to have a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you leave the map with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've seen the original of the document. We don't need it. We'll do with copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D88/3, and the explanation will be A and ter. Thank you. For the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, on this map we shall now try to find some buildings. Perhaps for the benefit of His Honour Judge Lindholm, who asked you where the building you lived in was, could you mark with the number 1 the building that you lived in and that you're still living in, I assume, in Pere Bosica Street.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this building has not been marked on the map, and it is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just put a number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Could you please mark the pensioners' home.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And put a number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you mean the pensioners' centre? Because we got "the pensioners' home".

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said home, the one the witness worked in. MR. DI FAZIO: [Previous translation continues] ... there's been reference to a place called the Spomen Dom, which appears at length throughout the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite a different matter. MR. DI FAZIO: [Previous translation continues] ... about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just the right moment for us to ask the witness to show us where this Spomen Dom is and to mark it with number 3.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Which means memorial centre. Tell me, please: Was there a Red Cross warehouse? How many there were? And if you could locate those Red Cross warehouses, that is, the warehouses of the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the town was shelled very frequently, in fact, daily, we decided to keep the foodstuffs of the Red Cross, the food supplies, in four different locations, for the simple reason that should one warehouse be hit and the food destroyed, something would be left intact. And we had four warehouses within the territory of the city. One was this building, DPO, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark it with the number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Another warehouse was across the road to the pensioners' centre. I think it is DS 17. Across the road here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put a number 5 there, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: There's no building drawn in here. [Marks] And the third warehouse was in the premises of the Velepromet company. No. I'm sorry. Agropromet. Agropromet. So should I put a number 6?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: [Marks] And number 7 would be the Uzarija company. I think it's here, but it hasn't been drawn in. I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just an approximate position will do, a number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, shall we say that the witness marked with number 1 the building he lived in; with the number 2, the pensioners' centre; number 3, the Spomen Dom or memorial centre; and number 4, 5, 6, and 7 mark the warehouses of the local Red Cross organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not need this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now a question for the witness: Do you know that in the vicinity of the buildings that you have just marked, some people got killed during shelling?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, between the pensioners' hall and the Red Cross warehouse - I don't know what number we used to mark it - a woman, a saleswoman, was killed. I think her name was Refika Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did she die?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: She died during shelling. She was killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to mark the map marked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought we have already numbered it, and the explanation was A.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now turn to another topic which touches upon the previous one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned shelling, and this is not a disputed fact in this case. How often were shellings -- you've already told us that, but I'm especially interested in May of 1992. Do you remember whether during that period of time there was shelling, and if so, what was the consequence of the shelling with respect to the institution where you worked?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In May of 1992 the shellings were very frequent, both during daytime and night-time. Life in town became increasingly difficult, and demands were voiced for citizens to be evacuated to leave the city. There were many casualties, and according to some data, most of the civilians and soldiers were killed during that year precisely. I know that during that month women and children left for Serbia. There were many demands for people to leave the town. However, our transportation means were very scarce. This was organised through the civil defence, and requests were sent into the Red Cross. I don't know exactly how many buses had left the city, but I know that a large group of women and children left in an organised fashion, and those who did not leave with them left in their own transportation means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Judge Lindholm has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me for interrupting you, but on the first line of the answer of the witness, it's page 68, line 25, he says: "In May of 1992, the shellings were very frequent." "Frequent" is not a very exact word. Were they daily, during day and night, and so on? Could you clarify that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've heard the question of Judge Lindholm. Could you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I said that the shellings were very frequent, regardless of whether it was day or night. It was constant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it daily?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the town shelled several times a day?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Several times a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that people applied to leave at the Red Cross, whereas the civil defence organised transportation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could now the witness be shown another document bearing internal number PDB 12/3? This is a list of refugees who left Bosanski Samac on the 17th of May, 1992. This document was issued by the Crisis Staff of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. Go over it. Do you know any of the people on this list, and is this in any way connected to what you just told us about evacuations to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know the majority of the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What is the ethnic composition of people on this list? Can you tell me approximately whether there are members of all three nations listed here?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are members of all three nations here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was drawn to the name under number 122, Petkovic Goran [as interpreted]. It says here that he was born in 1992. Does this mean that this was somebody just born that year when the evacuation took place, that this was a baby evacuated?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether this list pertains to residents of the entire Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, these are residents of the town itself and residents of villages that were shelled were allowed to leave in an organised fashion as well: Obudovac and other villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was their fate? What status did these people have after their leaving?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: We at the Red Cross were informed that these people were put up with their relatives, if they had such, and those that did not were housed in holding centres, accommodation centres in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another clarification. The first line here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is simply a clarification too. Mr. Lukic, on line 23, page 70, you say you're drawn to the name -- and 122, and it's written in the English translation as Petkovic Goran, but 122 is obviously a lady, Gordana Sedjic [phoen]. I presume it's 132, but it isn't a Petrovic anyway. It's a Nikolic. So just clarify that the child is that person and not the other one maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I said 132. I suppose that the interpreters misheard me. This is the person listed under number 132. The name is Goran Nikolic, so that we have no more mistakes here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, let's clarify this. This is entitled "The list of refugees." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these people were departing, were they citizens of Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that in this list there are some who were refugees from Croatia, but I'm not certain about this. I know a large majority of these people on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then could this document be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibits D89/3 and ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, after this evacuation of citizens to Serbia, was there any pressure exerted on the Red Cross and the civil defence staff in order to organise another evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The problems were not solved with this evacuation. On the contrary; after that, the number of citizens applying to leave the town grew after that. They wanted to go wherever it was possible, mostly to Serbia. And I don't think that -- we did not have other organised transports after that, and the reasons for that, as I was informed, was that these people could not find accommodation in Serbia, so that as a result of that, people left as they could, individually, upon receiving permits to leave municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued permits for leaving municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: As Your Honours please, as the transcript stands at the moment, it appears that because -- because they weren't organised transports, that was the reason people couldn't find accommodation in Serbia. It doesn't seem to make much sense as you read it. I wonder if that's what the witness intended to say, and in any event, it's a matter that should be clarified. It's obviously important. What was precisely the reason for their inability to go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I didn't say it in that way. I said that there were several reasons why we did not organise such types of evacuation of the population. One of the reasons was that we couldn't find transportation, and the other one is that these people could not be accommodated in Serbia. They could not accommodate this large number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that we couldn't organise again that this was the reason why they couldn't organise this evacuation again. However, the residents still applied to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: These people who came and applied to leave for Serbia, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: People of all ethnic backgrounds came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wishing to leave for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, wishing to leave there, for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about permits for leaving Samac. Do you know who issued them?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were issued by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody wanted to leave then to Croatia or to Gradacac, could one go there without any hindrance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Because there was a front line there. There was a front line between warring sides, so one couldn't go from one side to the other, regardless of any permits; one couldn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, something that is not directly linked to those first days of the conflict and for this indictment. Do you know something about whether some illegal or unlawful cases of leaving Samac in an organised way were set up?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I don't know much about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these people leaving to? Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: To Serbia. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it may be clear as between counsel and the witness, but as -- it's certainly not clear to me and I don't think it's very clear as one reads the transcript. First of all, what were these illegal or unlawful cases of leaving Samac? Why were they illegal or unlawful? And what's the relevance or the significance of the fact that they were going to Serbia, unless it's obvious to everyone else, it certainly isn't obvious to me, and I suggest that we should be clear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I think we do need clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we clarify this second question. Why did people want to leave Samac and go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Because the conditions of life became increasingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that people forged documents and permits in order to leave Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: This is how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this now clear sufficiently for the Prosecutor? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still in the month of May, and very briefly: Do you know what happened in early May in Odzak municipality? But in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I know that in the beginning of May in Odzak municipality people were captured, namely, a large -- Serbs, the Serbian population, was captured in large numbers, and these were Serbs who lived in the inhabited places of Novi Grad, Dubica, Trnjak, and the city of Odzak, town of Odzak itself. But mostly these were people from these inhabited places which I listed. So we had a very many demands, requests from members of their families from Samac who were inquiring after their relatives what had happened to these people who were taken prisoner in Odzak municipality, and these are two adjacent municipalities only divided by the river of Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," who were these applications sent to?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I mean the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time when the Serbs were taken prisoner in Odzak, was there an international institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer has not been recorded. When I said -- when I asked, when you say "we" who do you imply; you said the Red Cross, the local Red Cross chapter?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. I think apart from what you've just clarified, go on to your next question, and I think we need a clarification there, because it says, your question: "At that time when the Serbs were taken prisoner in Odzak, was there any international institution?" You might want to clarify which one you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that was the question I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the Serbs were detained in Odzak in May, was there an international institution -- did an international institution visit Samac, or you personally? Which one, when, why?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In May, the local Red Cross chapter was paid a visit by a lady, Mrs. or Ms., by the name of Kathy. She was a worker of the International Red Cross and she told me then that she had her offices in Tuzla. She also told me that she had been to Odzak and that she was expecting the issue of the captured Serbs in the area of Odzak municipality to be resolved. In which way, and how, that I don't know. But after a couple of days, she came to see me again and she asked for the local Red Cross organisation to get involved in the first exchange that had been agreed between the representatives of -- from Odzak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can he repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your last word "Samac"?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And Samac. From Odzak and Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did she do then, at that time? Did she undertake any organising preparations for that exchange? What do you know about the activities of this lady? Will you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, she brokered for this first exchange to be indeed carried out. She actually personally attended to that exchange. And she asked for the local Red Cross chapter to also be involved in that activity in order to help her. So it was she who exclusively organised that particular exchange. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the witness gave evidence that this exchange had been organised by local representatives -- I think the expression was local representatives from Samac and Odzak. If the witness knows who those representatives were, which persons or bodies, then that's obviously of significance in the case, and I think, I suggest to the Chamber that it would be a good idea if we knew exactly who he's talking about, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is more a matter for cross-examination, but I will seek to clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that she organised that exchange. Will you tell us: Was that particular exchange organised by her or by the local authorities in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I said that she had organised that exchange but that that exchange was -- had been the result of contacts between the municipality of Samac and representatives of the municipalities of Samac and those of Odzak. But the entire activity, the actual exchange itself, was organised by Ms. Katherine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To respond to the Prosecutor's question, do you know who was it from the Samac -- on behalf of Samac that had contacted the Odzak municipality people who were the actual persons involved?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the communications centre in that period, during those days?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: No, not in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know what it was that she specifically did in Samac? How did she liaise with the people? How did she get in touch with the actual people who were supposed to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I do not know exactly who it was that she negotiated with and agreed on the exchange and what the names of the people who were to be exchanged are. What I do know is that she came to the local Red Cross chapter and that she sought assistance for that activity to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that she went to see detention units in Samac at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of detention units in Samac at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I've heard about those. I heard about those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the concrete assistance that she asked you for, you individually?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that a number of old, elderly, and infirm people were supposed to be exchanged on that particular occasion and in view of the fact that that exchange was to take place under very unfavourable conditions, which is on the bank of the river and that we needed to ensure the basic prerequisites for that exchange to take place, namely, that we had to ensure stretchers to carry the old and infirm people, and there were some wounded people as well, and so ensure the necessary -- to provide the necessary boats to cross the river, as well as arrange for the welcome, the reception of the people that would be exchanged. So it was in this particular respect that both the civil defence and the Red Cross representatives actually contributed and helped to this particular exercise. Also people from the health service provided care, and the ambulance and other medical services required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where this exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: The exchange took place on the River Bosna, specifically in the village of Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date. It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention, page 79, line 15. The witness said this particular exchange, and the word used is "exercise."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were old people, infirm people. You're referring to people who were exchanged or people who were both leaving and those who were coming? So you were there on the spot, on the scene; is that not so? Describe the situation, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: At the request of Ms. Katherine, who asked for help from the local Red Cross, I personally, not wishing to expose any of my associates to any risks, I personally crossed the River Bosna in a boat to the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you had Red Cross equipment. Did you want to cross to the other bank with her or was there a decision or a request to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I did not want to. It's just that I wanted to accommodate her request, given the effort that she was making and given the risk that she was taking. So I wanted to help her carry out that particular exchange successfully, with all the help that I could give her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So without leading you, it was she who asked you to accompany her in the boat?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the actual exchange proceed? What did it look like? The Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that this was actually the first exchange which took place there after the beginning of the war. So how did it go?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Ms. Katherine told me that certain principles had been agreed upon, upon which this was to be done in the safest way possible. She told me that they had agreed with the other side that they were to provide one boat with the crew and that we were to provide another one, or the other one. As far as I know, they in the civil defence found such a boat and took it to the necessary spot. When we came to the river, on the other bank across the river, we saw that representatives from Odzak had already come there, but only uniformed soldiers, troops. I did not see any representatives of the Red Cross. And Mrs. Katherine objected to that, saying that the agreement had not been abided by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did she object? To whom did she address her objections?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: She objected to the representatives there who had come in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please clarify for the Trial Chamber: Who are they who is the opposite, the other side, and who was in uniform?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the representatives from Odzak, to people representing Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these soldiers in uniforms of the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. With this boat that we had brought there, Ms. Katherine and I crossed the Bosna River and we met with the representatives from Odzak. When she asked them why they hadn't brought a boat there, they replied that they didn't have one. However, they asserted that security would be guaranteed to all persons who would be exchanged on that occasion, as well as to representatives of the Red Cross, and that is indeed the way it was. The boat could seat five to six people, so we took five people from Odzak in one direction and then five people in the other direction. The conditions were extremely unfavourable. Access to the river was very forbidding, so that we had to carry people coming from Odzak to the bank on stretchers. And there were some people who had been wounded, who were wounded in the legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what condition were the people who were crossing from the Samac side to the Odzak side?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: As far as I could see, as I could see, no one was taken on a stretcher from that direction, but these were also elderly people, elderly people leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all these people from Samac cross over to the Odzak side? Were there any problems? And what was the principle of the exchange, or rather, what number had been had agreed to cross and to leave and to come?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Ms. Katherine, as far as I recollect, referred to the figure of 100 persons -- 100 to 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain, 100 for 100. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: 100 were to come and 100 were to leave. She also insisted that everybody had to state their views, to declare whether they indeed wanted to cross, and that referred to both groups on both banks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they state their views?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they said. They stated their options.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of them cross? Did all of them make the crossing?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I remember ten people from Samac did not cross over to the other side. They stated that they did not wish to go and they didn't cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the Odzak side?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: They didn't bring ten people from the other side, so it was 90 for 90.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they explain why they didn't send the ten people?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I had no occasion to ask them that, because I didn't see them. But Ms. Katherine spoke to them, and I don't know what was the answer that she received from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will be talking about the International Red Cross in some detail later on. Did you see Ms. Katherine again in the course of your work and contacts with representatives of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: After the exchange that she organised, I saw her only once again, and as far as I have been informed, she left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; not just she, but the International Red Cross. But soon after that, another representative of the Red Cross arrived. As far as I can remember, his name was Mattias Kind [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think it's time for us to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I would like to have an explanation of a part in the text which I don't have before me now in the transcript, but it runs like this: The access to the bank of the river was most forbidden. What does it mean? It's up on, I guess, on line 9 or 10 or something like that, on the foregoing page. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, Your Honour, that the error was in the transcript. The witness can explain, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say regarding access to the river?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC
utterances.text: I said it was difficult to have access to the bank, and also the separation line was right there. One side of the bank was held by one side, and the other by the other. So I said that it was forbidding, not forbidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: By the front line. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The River Bosna was in fact the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn until tomorrow at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
